content: Commissioned officer ranks in the Indian Army, from junior to senior: Lieutenant, Captain, Major, Lieutenant Colonel, Colonel, Brigadier, Major General, Lieutenant General and General. Field Marshal is a ceremonial five-star rank awarded rarely; only two officers (K. M. Cariappa and Sam Manekshaw) have held it.

Junior Commissioned Officers (JCOs) are Naib Subedar, Subedar and Subedar Major. Non-Commissioned Officers (NCOs) are Lance Naik, Naik and Havildar. The entry-level soldier rank is Sepoy in infantry, with different names in other arms (for example Gunner in artillery, Sapper in engineers and Sowar in armoured regiments).

Army Day is celebrated every year on 15 January. It marks the day in 1949 when Lieutenant General K. M. Cariappa took over as the first Indian Commander-in-Chief of the Indian Army from General Sir Francis Butcher.

The Indian Army is organised into seven commands: six operational commands (Northern, Western, South Western, Southern, Central and Eastern) and the Army Training Command (ARTRAC). Each is headed by a Lieutenant General.

Wartime gallantry awards in order of precedence are the Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra and Vir Chakra. Peacetime gallantry awards are the Ashoka Chakra, Kirti Chakra and Shaurya Chakra. The Param Vir Chakra is the highest wartime award and the Ashoka Chakra is the highest peacetime award.

The post of Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) was created in 2019 to provide single-point military advice to the government and improve coordination between the Army, Navy and Air Force. General Bipin Rawat was the first CDS, taking office on 1 January 2020.

India shares land borders with Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. The total land border is roughly 15,000 km. The border with Pakistan in Jammu and Kashmir is called the Line of Control (LoC), and the de facto border with China is called the Line of Actual Control (LAC).
source: Ministry of Home Affairs / Ministry of External Affairs - verify

content: Siachen is a glacier in the Karakoram range at an altitude above about 5,000 metres and is often described as the world's highest battlefield. Troops there face extreme cold, avalanches, crevasses and altitude illness, which cause more casualties than combat.
The Army Act 1950 is the law governing discipline, service conditions and trial of offences for personnel of the Indian Army. The full text is available on India Code (indiacode.nic.in).

Under the Army Act, offences by service personnel are tried by courts martial. The four types are General Court Martial, District Court Martial, Summary General Court Martial and Summary Court Martial, differing in the powers of punishment they can award.

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation) is India's regional satellite navigation system developed by ISRO. It covers India and an area extending about 1,500 km around it, and provides position information for civilian and restricted military use.

A compass needle points to magnetic north, which differs from true north by an angle called magnetic declination. To take a bearing, point the direction-of-travel arrow at the target, rotate the bezel until the north marker aligns with the needle, and read the bearing at the index line. A back bearing is the bearing plus or minus 180 degrees.

content: On a military or survey map, give the easting (vertical grid line number, read left to right) first and the northing (horizontal line number, read bottom to top) second. A six-figure grid reference locates a point to within 100 metres.

On a 1:50,000 map, 1 cm equals 500 m on the ground; on a 1:25,000 map, 1 cm equals 250 m. Contour lines close together show steep ground, widely spaced lines show gentle slopes, and closed circles show hilltops.

Common camouflage principles are to avoid shape, shadow, shine, silhouette, spacing and movement. Break up the outline, use natural vegetation and local colours, keep out of skylines and avoid reflective surfaces.

The safest way to treat suspect water is to bring it to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute (3 minutes above about 2,000 metres altitude), then let it cool. Filters and purification tablets can also be used, following the product instructions.
source: WHO / CDC water treatment guidance - verify

content: A common survival rule of thumb is that a person can survive about 3 minutes without air, 3 hours in harsh weather without shelter, 3 days without water and 3 weeks without food. This means priorities are safety, shelter, water, then food.

Acute mountain sickness (AMS) can occur above about 2,500 metres and causes headache, nausea, fatigue, dizziness and poor sleep. Treatment is to stop climbing, rest, drink fluids and descend if symptoms worsen. Prevention is gradual ascent with rest days and avoiding rapid height gain.

High altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE) shows as breathlessness at rest, cough, and sometimes pink frothy sputum. High altitude cerebral oedema (HACE) shows as confusion, loss of balance and drowsiness. Both are emergencies: descend immediately, give oxygen if available and get urgent medical help.

Signs of hypothermia include shivering, confusion, slurred speech and drowsiness. Move the casualty to shelter, remove wet clothing, insulate from the ground, wrap in dry layers and give warm sweet drinks only if fully conscious. Handle gently, do not rub the limbs and seek medical help.
source: Red Cross / MedlinePlus first aid guidance - verify

content: Frostbitten skin looks white, waxy and feels numb. Do not rub it. Rewarm only if there is no risk of refreezing, using warm (not hot) water at about 37 to 39 degrees Celsius, and protect the area with dry loose dressings. Seek medical care.
source: Red Cross / MedlinePlus first aid guidance - verify

content: Heat exhaustion causes heavy sweating, weakness, headache and nausea. Heat stroke is an emergency, with body temperature above about 40 degrees Celsius and confusion or collapse. Move to shade, cool the body quickly with water and fanning, give fluids if conscious, and get urgent medical help.
source: Red Cross / WHO first aid guidance - verify

content: Signs of dehydration include thirst, dark urine, dizziness and fatigue. Treat with oral rehydration solution (ORS), made with the correct amounts of salt and sugar in clean water, and small frequent sips. Severe dehydration needs medical care.

Apply firm direct pressure to the wound with a clean pad and keep the pressure on. If bleeding from a limb is life-threatening and pressure fails, apply a tourniquet above the wound (not on a joint), tighten until bleeding stops, and note the time applied. Get medical help urgently.

For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally, call for emergency help and start chest compressions in the centre of the chest at 100 to 120 per minute, about 5 to 6 cm deep, letting the chest rise fully between presses. If trained, give 2 breaths after every 30 compressions.
source: Red Cross / resuscitation council guidance - verify

content: Keep the casualty calm and still, immobilise the bitten limb, remove rings and tight items, and get to a hospital quickly for antivenom. Do not cut the wound, suck the venom, apply ice or use a tight tourniquet.

Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes, remove rings and clothing near the burn unless stuck to it, and cover loosely with a clean non-fluffy dressing. Do not use ice, butter or toothpaste. Seek medical help for large, deep or facial burns.
source: Red Cross first aid guidance - verify

content: Suspect a fracture if there is pain, swelling, deformity or inability to use the limb. Keep the limb still, support it with a splint that includes the joints above and below the injury, check circulation beyond the splint, and get medical help. Cover open wounds with a clean dressing.
source: Red Cross first aid guidance - verify

content: Signs of stress or poor mental health include poor sleep, irritability, withdrawal, loss of interest and heavy drinking. Talking to a trusted comrade, supervisor or medical officer early helps, and anyone in crisis should be taken seriously and connected to professional help immediately.
